title: What is caching in Spring Boot (@Cacheable/@CachePut/@CacheEvict)? When to use Redis? L1 vs L2 cache? What is cache stampede and how to prevent it? TTL strategy? Cache key design? Redis data structures? Redis distributed lock? What to do when Redis is unavailable?
shortTitle: What is Spring Cache with Redis?
keyPoints: @Cacheable implements cache-aside for reads: check cache first, on miss execute the method and store the result
@CacheEvict removes stale entries when data changes; @CachePut always executes and updates the cache
Redis is the standard distributed cache: in-memory, sub-millisecond, shared across all service instances
Cache keys must include ALL inputs that change the response, including tenantId, accountId, and pagination
Every cached entry needs a TTL; different data types need different TTLs based on volatility
Cache stampede occurs when many requests miss the same expired key simultaneously; fix with distributed lock and TTL jitter
When Redis is unavailable, the circuit breaker trips and the service falls back to direct database queries

s1_definition.oneliner: @Cacheable checks the cache before executing a method and stores the result on a miss, @CacheEvict removes stale entries when data changes, and Redis provides a distributed cache shared across all service instances with sub-millisecond access.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **@Cacheable** – implements the cache-aside pattern for reads: if the cache has the value, return it immediately without executing the method; if not, execute the method, store the result, and return it.
- **@CachePut** – always executes the method and writes the result into the cache, keeping the cache in sync after writes.
- **@CacheEvict** – removes one or all entries from a cache region when data changes, so the next read fetches the fresh value.
- **Redis** – an in-memory data store used as a distributed cache: sub-millisecond latency, shared across all service instances, supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, and sorted sets.
- **Cache stampede** – when many requests simultaneously miss the same expired key and all hit the database at once.
- **TTL (Time To Live)** – the maximum duration a cached entry is valid before automatic expiration.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a copy of frequently requested exchange rates at the front desk (cache) instead of calling the forex desk (database) every time. @Cacheable means check the front desk copy first; if it is not there, call the forex desk and bring a copy back. @CacheEvict means the forex desk just updated a rate, so throw away the front desk copy so the next customer gets the fresh one. Cache stampede: 100 customers ask for the USD rate at the exact moment the front desk copy expires, and all 100 rush to the forex desk simultaneously.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring Cache provides @Cacheable for cache-aside reads (check cache, miss triggers the method and stores the result), @CachePut for updating the cache after a write (always executes and refreshes), and @CacheEvict for invalidating stale entries. Redis is the standard distributed cache at National Bank of India: in-memory sub-millisecond access, shared across all service instances, with JSON serialization so cache entries survive code changes.

Every cached entry needs a TTL. Different data gets different TTLs: exchange rates at 60 seconds, account balances at 10 seconds, customer profiles at 15 minutes, and reference data at 24 hours. For stampede prevention when a hot key expires and 500 requests arrive simultaneously, Rajesh uses a Redis distributed lock (SET NX PX) so only one instance fetches from the database while others wait and read from cache. TTL jitter spreads expirations over time so keys do not all expire at the same instant.

The most important principle is resilience: a cache outage should degrade performance, never cause a total outage. When Redis is unavailable, the GracefulCacheErrorHandler logs the error and the service falls back to direct database queries. Priya sees her balance either way; only the speed changes.

Remember one sentence: @Cacheable checks cache before executing, @CacheEvict removes stale entries on write, Redis shares the cache across all instances, and every entry needs a TTL with jitter to prevent stampede.
